newsitem.title: SURINAM: Surinamese pyramid savers demand government's help.
newsitem.headline: Surinamese pyramid savers demand government's help.

text.p: About 300 angry Surinamese marched to the office of the president on Friday to demand government help after a local businessman said he could not pay back money they had invested in a pyramid savings scheme.
The collapse of the get-rich-quick scheme on Wednesday has led to fears of widespread violence in the former Dutch colony as occurred in Albania, where similar schemes failed in April.
A delegation of depositors led by Stanley Brug was met by President Jules Wijdenbosch's spokesman Andy Rusland who told them the government was still considering its options.
"We are looking for solutions to the problem," Rusland said.

Local economists say the saving schemes -- which rely on ever increasing numbers of depositors to pay off old investors -- contain at least half the amount of savings in commercial banks and that many investors have borrowed heavily to take advantage of the 120 percent annual interest rates they offered.
Local banks offer rates of less than 20 percent per year.

An angry mob of about 200 investors hurled insults outside the offices of Roep NV, the biggest of Suriname's pyramid schemes which announced on Wednesday that it needed one to three years to pay back their money.
"If I don't get my money back, I'll make sure Roep loses everything," one middle aged man shouted.
About 15 police officers stood guard around the building.

Government officials in the South American country of 430,000 people have made few comments on the crisis, which local economists have called a timebomb, other than a vague commitment to protect small investors.
